title: Max Walks for Ruby Bridges
author: Shellfie original
credit: An original story written for the McKinley Bulldogs. Historical facts about Ruby Bridges are drawn from widely published sources.

pages: One morning in November, Max puts on a purple shirt, a purple hat, and purple socks. Today is Ruby Bridges Walk to School Day, and McKinley families are meeting at Paloma Park to walk to school together. Grandma asks, "Do you know why we wear purple?" Max shrugs. "I know it's for Ruby Bridges, but I don't know her whole story." So as they walk, Grandma tells it.

In 1960, many schools in the southern United States were segregated. That means Black children and white children were not allowed to go to the same schools. A court ordered the schools in New Orleans to change. On November 14, 1960, a six-year-old girl named Ruby Bridges became the first Black student at William Frantz Elementary School.

Some adults were very angry about the change. On Ruby's first days, crowds stood outside the school yelling cruel things. Four United States marshals, who are federal officers, walked beside Ruby to keep her safe. Many white families pulled their children out of the school, so Ruby spent most of that year as the only student in her class.

But Ruby had a teacher named Barbara Henry, who taught her every single day. Ruby kept coming to school, kept learning, and even prayed for the people who shouted at her. Her courage helped open the door for children of every race to learn together. Years later, the artist Norman Rockwell painted a famous picture of Ruby walking to school between the marshals.

When they reach McKinley, Max looks around at the crowd of families in purple. Kids of every color and background are laughing and walking into the same school, through the same gate. "Ruby was only a little older than a kindergartner," Max says quietly. "She was so brave." Grandma nods. "She was. And every time we walk together, we remember that school belongs to everyone."
